title: A Once 'Undruggable' Pancreatic Cancer Target Falls: New Drug Nearly Doubles Survival
summary: Pancreatic cancer has long been one of oncology's most formidable foes. With a five-year survival rate of just 3% for metastatic disease, it kills approximately 97% of patients within five years of diagnosis. The central culprit is a mutation in the KRAS gene, present in over 90% of cases, which acts like a stuck accelerator pedal, commanding cells to divide uncontrollably. For decades, KRAS was considered "undruggable"—its smooth surface offered no obvious crevice for a drug to bind. That narrative shattered on May 31, 2026, when Revolution Medicines presented Phase 3 data on daraxonrasib. This once-daily pill doesn't target KRAS directly; instead, it binds to cyclophilin A, a cellular chaperone that helps fold proteins. The resulting complex then attaches to active KRAS and silences its cancer-driving signals. The trial enrolled 500 patients with metastatic pancreatic cancer who had already received prior treatment. The results were striking: daraxonrasib extended median overall survival from 6.7 months with standard chemotherapy to 13.2 months—a near doubling—and reduced the risk of death by 60%. While side effects were notable, including a prominent rash in 86% of patients and stomatitis (painful mouth sores), patients on daraxonrasib were far less likely to discontinue treatment due to toxicity and reported better quality of life with reduced pain. "This milestone represents a likely shift in pancreatic cancer treatment," says Dr. Christopher Lieu, a gastrointestinal oncologist. The company will now seek expedited approval from the FDA and other regulators. If approved, the drug could reach clinics within months. Beyond this immediate victory, the success opens the door for combination therapies pairing KRAS inhibitors with other agents to forestall resistance, potentially ushering in a new era of precision medicine for one of the world's deadliest cancers.
why_it_matters: For a cancer that historically offers few survivors, a near-doubling of survival time is a profound step. This breakthrough also validates the strategy of targeting 'undruggable' proteins by co-opting helper molecules, which could inspire similar tactics against other hard-to-treat cancers, altering how medicine tackles genetic diseases.

background_read: Pancreatic cancer is often diagnosed at a late stage because it shows few symptoms early on; by the time it is found, the tumor is usually metastatic, which is why the overall 5-year survival rate is only about 13%—and drops to 3% for metastatic disease.

The KRAS gene encodes a signaling protein that acts like a switch for cell growth; when mutated, the switch gets stuck 'on,' relentlessly driving cell division—this was first discovered in 1982 and has frustrated drug developers ever since.

In 2021, the first-ever KRAS inhibitor, sotorasib, was approved for a specific KRAS G12C mutation in lung cancer, but it does not work in pancreatic cancer because the prevalent mutation there is G12D, which daraxonrasib targets by binding cyclophilin A.

Revolution Medicines, a clinical-stage biotech firm, designed daraxonrasib (formerly RMC-9805) as a ‘molecular glue’—it forces cyclophilin A to stick to active KRAS, blocking its cancer-driving signals without needing a traditional binding pocket.

If the FDA grants accelerated approval based on the Phase 3 data, it could become the standard of care for second-line pancreatic cancer, and combination trials with other targeted drugs are already planned to prevent resistance and push survival beyond one year.
Article_Structure: LEAD: Pancreatic cancer's grim survival stats (3% for metastatic disease) set up the problem.
└─ CULPRIT: Mutation in KRAS gene (over 90% of cases) acts as a stuck accelerator.
OBSTACLE: For decades, KRAS was considered 'undruggable' due to its smooth protein surface.
BREAKTHROUGH: On May 31, 2026, Revolution Medicines announced Phase 3 results for daraxonrasib.
MECHANISM: The drug binds cyclophilin A, a chaperone; the resulting complex silences active KRAS.
CLINICAL DATA: 500 previously treated patients: median survival doubled from 6.7 to 13.2 months; death risk reduced 60%.
├─ SIDE EFFECTS: Rash (86%), stomatitis, but less treatment discontinuation and better quality of life.
QUOTE: Dr. Christopher Lieu calls it a likely shift in pancreatic cancer treatment.
NEXT STEPS: Company seeks expedited FDA approval; drug could reach clinics within months.
FUTURE: Success opens door for combination therapies to block resistance, potentially transforming precision medicine for deadly cancers.

perspectives.description: Patients and doctors welcome a new oral therapy that not only extends life but also improves pain and quality, offering a lifeline where palliative options were previously limited; the drug's targeted approach may reduce reliance on harsh chemotherapy.

While a survival increase to 13.2 months is significant, it is still measured in months, and the severe rash and mouth sores affect a large majority; some worry that accelerated approval might skip long-term safety data and that drug pricing could place it out of reach for many patients.

Historically, progress in pancreatic cancer has been slow and incremental; daraxonrasib illustrates a broader trend of targeting molecular chaperones as a back door to attack previously 'undruggable' targets, a paradigm shift that stretches back to the first KRAS inhibitor approval in 2021 and may extend to other KRAS-mutant cancers like colorectal and lung.

Future research will focus on combining daraxonrasib with other drugs to delay resistance, and the concept of using cyclophilin A as a scaffold could be adapted to silence other hard-to-drug proteins, potentially leading to a new class of cancer therapies that turn the 'undruggable' into routine targets.
